question: What is the main difference between localized cancer treatments and systemic treatments?

options.A: Localized treatments are always surgical while systemic treatments are always oral
options.B: Systemic therapies only affect the specific organ where the tumor originally started
options.C: Systemic therapies travel through the bloodstream to reach cells throughout the body
options.D: Localized treatments cure cancer completely while systemic treatments only relieve pain

explanation: You've got this! Systemic treatments enter the bloodstream, which lets them reach cancer cells that might have traveled away from the main tumor site.

question: Why is it important for nurses to know if a cancer treatment is meant to cure the disease or provide comfort (palliative)?

options.A: It dictates whether the patient is allowed to receive any form of nutrition by mouth
options.B: Palliative regimens mean the patient no longer requires physical assessments or lab work
options.C: Curative regimens require nurses to administer medications without checking vital signs
options.D: It helps guide realistic patient expectations, monitoring priorities, and supportive care planning

explanation: Great nursing insight! Knowing the main goal of treatment helps you plan the best supportive care and keep patient expectations clear and hopeful.

question: Why does chemotherapy often cause hair loss and upset stomach lining?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs specifically seek out and destroy healthy tissues
options.B: These areas of the body have a much higher temperature than others
options.C: Patients fail to eat enough nutritious food during their hospital stay
options.D: These normal tissues consist of cells that divide very rapidly

explanation: Spot on! Chemo targets fast-dividing cells. Because our hair and gut lining naturally grow fast, they get affected too along with the cancer cells.

question: A nurse is about to give a vesicant chemo drug through a hand vein. What is the most crucial check before starting?

options.A: Instructing the patient to tightly flex their arm muscles throughout the entire infusion
options.B: Warming the intravenous fluid bag to body temperature to prevent vein spasms
options.C: Verifying brisk blood return to confirm the catheter is properly placed inside the vein
options.D: Diluting the concentrated medication with sterile water instead of normal saline

explanation: Wonderful safety check! Vesicants can severely damage surrounding skin if they leak, so always check for blood return first to make sure you are safely in the vein.

question: How do targeted therapy drugs differ from traditional chemotherapy?

options.A: They work exclusively by boosting the overall white blood cell count in the bloodstream
options.B: They can only be taken as topical creams applied directly to skin lesions
options.C: They completely rebuild the patient's bone marrow within forty-eight hours of administration
options.D: They focus on specific molecular targets involved in tumor growth rather than attacking all dividing cells

explanation: You're doing great! Targeted therapies act like smart missiles, zeroing in on specific cancer proteins instead of harming all fast-growing cells.

question: Which of these is NOT a typical side effect of immune checkpoint inhibitors?

options.A: Inflammation of the colon leading to severe diarrhea
options.C: Permanent structural damage to the heart muscle valves
options.D: Dermatitis and itchy rashes across the skin surface

explanation: You got this right! These drugs ramp up the immune system, causing inflammatory side effects like rashes or gut issues, but heart valve destruction isn't a hallmark of this class.

question: What is the main goal of hormone therapy in certain cancers?

options.A: To permanently increase the patient's natural testosterone and estrogen levels
options.B: To block or lower hormone levels that stimulate the growth of hormone-sensitive tumors
options.C: To completely replace failing endocrine glands throughout the entire body
options.D: To stimulate rapid production of red blood cells to prevent severe anemia

explanation: Exactly! Some cancers love hormones to grow. Hormone therapy cuts off that fuel supply to slow them down.

question: A patient on hormone therapy for prostate cancer reports hot flashes and fatigue. How should you understand these symptoms?

options.A: Evidence of severe bone marrow suppression caused by the treatment
options.B: Early indicators of metastatic cancer spreading to the brain
options.C: Signs of an acute allergic reaction to the oral medication
options.D: Expected side effects resulting from artificially lowered hormone levels

explanation: Spot on! Lowering hormones mimics natural changes like menopause or andropause, which often brings tiredness and hot flashes.

question: How does external radiation therapy primarily destroy cancer cells?

options.A: By using high-energy rays to damage cellular DNA and stop cell division
options.B: By lowering the patient's core body temperature to induce cellular death
options.C: By surgically removing the affected organ through a small skin incision
options.D: By flooding the circulatory system with cytotoxic chemical compounds

explanation: Well done! Radiation uses targeted high-energy beams to break the DNA inside cancer cells so they can't multiply anymore.

question: A patient receiving neck radiation asks if they can use their favorite scented lotion on the area. What is the best reply?

options.A: Recommend using only approved, gentle, fragrance-free products to avoid further skin irritation
options.B: Suggest stopping all skin hygiene practices until the entire course of treatment finishes
options.C: Advise scrubbing the skin firmly with a washcloth before applying any cream or lotion
options.D: Encourage applying the scented lotion generously right before each radiation session

explanation: You're thinking like a caring nurse! Radiation makes skin very sensitive, so stick to mild, fragrance-free lotions approved by the care team.

question: Why is a low white blood cell count (neutropenia) a medical emergency for patients on chemotherapy?

options.A: It prevents the kidneys from filtering normal metabolic waste products
options.B: It leads to severe joint stiffness and sudden hair loss across the scalp
options.C: The body loses its primary defense against invading bacteria and pathogens
options.D: It causes immediate, uncontrollable bleeding from small skin cuts

explanation: Spot on! Neutrophils are our infection-fighting soldiers. When they drop, even minor germs can quickly cause serious infections.

question: A patient undergoing chemotherapy has a platelet count of 45,000/mcL. Which instruction is best?

options.A: Increase intake of green leafy vegetables to boost iron and clotting factors
options.B: Take high-dose aspirin daily to help thin the blood and improve circulation
options.C: Perform vigorous deep-tissue stretching exercises twice a day to prevent stiffness
options.D: Use an electric shaver instead of a traditional razor for daily grooming

explanation: Brilliant! Low platelets mean a higher risk of bleeding, so switching from sharp razors to electric shavers helps keep the patient safe from cuts.

question: What is the main cause of Tumor Lysis Syndrome when cancer treatment begins?

options.A: Rapid destruction of large numbers of cancer cells releasing contents into the blood
options.B: Bacterial invasion of the bloodstream due to low white blood cell counts
options.C: Severe dehydration caused by prolonged nausea and vomiting after chemotherapy
options.D: A sudden allergic reaction to the intravenous fluids administered in the clinic

explanation: You've got this! When chemo works *too* fast, cells burst open all at once, flooding the blood with waste products that stress the kidneys.

question: A lung cancer patient reports sudden back pain, weak legs, and trouble passing urine. What emergency should you suspect?
explanation: Excellent clinical catch! Back pain plus weakness and bladder issues is a classic red flag for a tumor pressing right on the spinal cord.

question: When can palliative care start for a patient with advanced cancer?

options.A: At any point during the illness, alongside active curative treatments
options.B: Only when the patient is completely free of all physical pain
options.C: Exclusively during the final forty-eight hours of life in a hospice unit
options.D: Only after all forms of chemotherapy and radiation have failed

explanation: Wonderful to know! Palliative care isn't just for end-of-life; it can start right from diagnosis to help manage symptoms and boost quality of life.

question: A patient with advanced cancer starts strong opioid pain medication. What preventive care must you include?

options.A: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload from the oral medications
options.B: Encouraging a low-fiber diet to reduce gastrointestinal activity during treatment
options.C: Checking blood pressure every fifteen minutes to monitor for sudden hypertension
options.D: Administering prescribed stool softeners and laxatives to prevent opioid-induced constipation

explanation: Spot on! Opioids slow down the bowels significantly. Always team them up with a laxative to keep the patient comfortable and safe from constipation.
